A 10% increase in public school spending led to ca 7% higher wages, 3.2 percentage point reduction in adult poverty and 0.31 more completed years of education
So the countries that spend a small fraction of what USA does on education have much higher scores because...?

While I won't disagree with the fact that we spend way too much money for our shitty education system there is a good reason we spend more per capita than other countries, and deliver poor results for it.

You have to remember how large the United States is and how low our population density is compared to most other major countries. In most European countries, for example, you have a handful of major cities which contain a large portion of the population. The Paris metropolitan area contains ~1/5 of the population of the entire country.

There are a number of reasons this is important:

  • Logistics

Having a large portion of your population in a small area will help avoid a number of logistical issues. (i.e. You need to make sure students can actually access the school (distance) or that you have transportation for them. Also there is the consideration of infrastructure, which would already exist in a major metropolitan area but might not in a rural area)

  • Geographic cultural differences

Geography tends to play a part in diversity of thought and culture. People in the SE US don't really interact all that much with people in the NE or on the West coast. As a result we've developed very distinct cultural attitudes and this affects how we educate our children. Some people want creation science taught in school alongside evolution. Others don't. Attempting to accommodate numerous attitudes within the education system leads to greater complexity and more expense as a result. However, when people cluster together in urban or small geographic areas they tend to develop a more conformist culture, and are easier to accommodate.

  • Locality

Because of the different cultural differences noted above, people tend to demand more local control of their educational system. Aside from the complexity issue this tends to lead to a problem with consistency of education. A in the boondocks of Louisiana will not have the same funding or brainpower as a school in Boston and will be unlikely to provide the same level of education, and there is a very good chance the residents of the area, who went through the same educational system themselves, are ignorant enough to not realize just how terrible their educational system is. And even if they did it is unlikely they have any means to improve the situation.

When you take the above into consideration you can really start to understand why so many social systems that work for our European counterparts fail in the US. People talk about how much we spend on healthcare, for example, compared to other countries but I'm very skeptical that a European style universal coverage system would work as well in the US as it does in Europe for the same reasons listed above.

In fact, because of funding problems France had to close a number of hospitals a few years back. Of course, they didn't close hospitals major metro areas, they closed hospitals in sparsely populated rural areas. They were used far less than the metro area hospitals and cost far more to maintain per capita.
